artboards.title: Proposed — no meeting yet, and no memory

annotations.text:
WHAT I TOOK FROM YOUR ANSWERS

You told me four things and every decision here follows from them.

THE SCREEN IS THE MANAGER'S RECORD, not the morning console. The conversation lives in the panel on all forty screens; this screen is the ledger of the relationship. So it now opens with a VERDICT — five figures that say what this manager has been worth — and that strip is the thing the screen never had.

ONE RECORD, BEHIND A SWITCH. Twelve flat sections become two beds: Standing (what still wants an answer from you) and The record (what it has advised since June, and what followed). "The last meeting", "The weekly review" and "Earlier meetings" are one journal. "Advice you passed on", "Advice that is not landing" and "What has worked, and what has not" are one table with a filter — the code's own comment says they are the same question asked three ways.

DESKTOP AT THE DESK. The console is drawn properly at 1440; the phone is drawn from scratch at 390 as its own design, but it carries the plan and the switch and nothing more.

DESIGN CANVAS FIRST. Nothing in index.html has been touched. Every value here is lifted from the app's own source: the 23-colour palette, the 11/12/13/14 type ramp, Inter + Archivo Black + IBM Plex Mono, and the .ow-* console components already shipping on Today, Debtors, Creditors, Purchase invoices and the cash book. No new colour, no fourteenth button family, no half-pixel type.

WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT AS IT STANDS →

1. TWELVE SECTIONS OF EQUAL WEIGHT. Today's plan, the last meeting, the scoreboard, the questions, the weekly review, earlier meetings, advice passed on, advice not landing, what has worked, the playbook, the standing rules. Every one gets the same 15px grey heading, the same 12px card, the same rounded box. The screen has no opinion about what matters, so the eye has none either.

2. NOTHING SAYS WHETHER THIS MANAGER IS ANY GOOD. The whole screen is about advice and there is not one figure anywhere that answers "has it earned its credit?". You have to read nine sections and add up.

3. FIVE MOVES COST 700px. A move card is a title, a 176-character unmeasured paragraph and three buttons, at about 140px each. Four moves fill the first screen; the fifth is below the fold. The paragraph runs the full 1,140px of the column with no measure at all — the single worst thing about the app before the console.

4. NINE OXIDE BUTTONS ON ONE PAGE. Draft the chase, Draft the order, Draft the follow-up, Open pricing, Take it on, Answer, Answer, Try it, Talk to it. The palette's own rule is that the accent appears ONCE, on the one thing to do next. Here it appears nine times, which means it appears nowhere.

5. AMBER INK ON THE MONEY. .mgr-worth and .mgr-target-fig are --accent-ink, which is the amber ink. A figure is a size, not a warning — and this is the exact pairing the design system names as already shipped and wrong.

6. THE MONEY IS NOT MONOSPACED. .mgr-worth and .mgr-target-fig set no font-family, so 1,420,000 and 214,000 render in Inter, do not sit in a column, and cannot be compared down the page. Every figure in this app is meant to be IBM Plex Mono with tabular numerals.

7. THE MEETING OFFER IS A 90px BOX with a 56-character paragraph, a button, a dashed rule and a second button — above the plan, on a screen opened every morning for months, saying the same three sentences every time.

8. THE TWO-COLUMN GRID IS RAGGED. The sections are flat siblings dropped into halves, so a short one leaves a 200px hole beside a tall one, and the reading order zig-zags: scoreboard, questions, review, earlier meetings, passed on, not landing, what worked.

9. THREE SECTIONS ASK ONE QUESTION. Passed on, not landing, what has worked. Each has its own heading, its own 250-word explanation and its own row format, and the answer is in a different shape in each.

10. THE RECORD IS ALL PROSE, NO SPINE. "chased 7 times, paid inside 3 days 5 of them" is a good sentence, but there is no column to sort, filter or scan — so a shop with eleven levers reads eleven sentences.

11. OFF-SYSTEM VALUES: 12.5 / 13.5 / 14.5px type, weight 650 and 700 where the ramp says 600, radius 10 and 12 where the system has 4 / 6 / 8, and a dashed border used as an ornament.

THE PROPOSAL — what changed, and why

WHAT READS FIRST IS THE VERDICT. Five figures across a 64px strip: advice done, targets met, levers that work, advice not landing, meetings held. This is the thing the old screen could not say. Each is derivable from what the journal already stores — managerAdviceTally, managerTrackRecord and the score reading already compute every one of them. Nothing is coloured except "not landing", which is amber because advice that reaches nobody is a real fault; the rest are ink, because a figure is a size, not a warning.

TWO BEDS, ONE SWITCH. Standing is what still wants an answer from you. The record is what it has advised and what followed. The switch is the same segmented control the cash book uses for its account filter — not a fourteenth component.

A MOVE IS A ROW, NOT A CARD. Title (who first, like the cash book row), kind, and the money in mono on the right. Five moves are 220px instead of 700px, and the whole plan sits above the fold with the playbook under it. The one you are working on OPENS IN PLACE and gets the space a decision deserves: the reasoning at a 76ch measure, an evidence line — invoiced, last chased, paid within three days 5 of 7, their whole balance — and the actions with the skip reason as a field beside Skip rather than a modal after it.

THE ACCENT IS THE OPEN MOVE'S ACTION, ONCE. "Draft the chase" is the only oxide thing on the screen. The meeting has been held, so "Hold another anyway" is a ghost button in a quiet panel footer where it belongs, with the credit warning as the footer's own sentence. On the record view the single accent is "Hold the weekly review", because looking back IS the act there. On the un-held morning it is "Hold the morning meeting".

THE MONEY IS MONO, TABULAR, AND RIGHT-ALIGNED. 1,420,000 / 3,180,000 / 860,000 / 214,000 line up as a column you can read down. The basis sits under each figure in 11px Inter. A move the books cannot size says so — "nothing on file to size it" — rather than printing a number nobody can stand behind.

THE JOURNAL IS ONE LIST. Meetings and weekly reviews are the same kind of event on the same clock, newest first, each a 44px row: date, what it was about, and how much of it got done. A review opens to its week table and its lessons. Three sections become one, and "3 mornings had no meeting" is said in the footer rather than left as a gap you have to count.

EVERY LEVER IT HAS PULLED is the whole of the old three-section record, in one table with one filter: All, Works, Never worked, Not landing, You passed on. The verdict column carries the sentence the old sections carried; the chip says which kind; the Worked column is the only coloured thing in the table, verdigris where it works and crimson where it never has. The caveat the code already writes — counted once per occasion, nine older moves name nothing the books could follow — sits under the table instead of above it.

THE RAIL CARRIES WHAT IS SMALL AND STANDING. Scoreboard with pace, the two questions it needs answered with the field right there, and the standing rules as three figure rows. On the record the rail carries the account of the whole relationship — 142 moves proposed, 58 done, 27 skipped with a reason, 57 never touched — and says out loud that 57 untouched is a fact about the meeting, not about you.

THE PLAYBOOK STAYS BESIDE THE WORK, not in the record, because a play is live: each row carries its span clock, and one past its own span goes oxide, which is the manager's failure to answer for, not the shop's.

WHAT I HAVE NOT DECIDED FOR YOU

1. THE FIFTH STRIP CELL. I chose "meetings held". The other candidate was money — what moved alongside its advice — and I left it out because the app's own law is that movement is never credit, and a single money figure in a verdict strip would read as credit however it was labelled. If you want it, it belongs as a rail line on the record with the "alongside it, never because of it" wording.

2. "NOT LANDING" IS THE ONE AMBER CELL. It is the only place on the strip where I let colour in. The argument for it: advice put to you six times and never answered is the manager wasting your mornings. The argument against: it is a fact about the machine, not about the shop, and the strip is otherwise about the shop. One line to change.

3. THE SWITCH IS TWO ITEMS, NOT THREE. The playbook and the standing rules sit under Standing because they are live. A case exists for a third bed, "How it works", holding both plus the questions. I did not take it because three tabs on a screen with two real jobs is a filing system, not a design.

4. WHERE THE WEEKLY REVIEW IS HELD FROM. I put the button in the journal's own header, on the record view. It is currently in the meeting box at the top of the page. If you hold reviews on a Monday morning without going looking for them, it may want to be in the page header beside Talk to it — but then Standing has two accents.

5. THE LEVERS TABLE SHOWS 6 OF 11 and says so. I did not build the "show all" behaviour, or decide whether the filter chips should also re-sort. Eleven rows fits; forty would not.

6. THE PHONE CARRIES STANDING ONLY in what I drew. The record on a phone is the same journal and the same table at 15px, which works, but you said desktop is where you use this — so I have not spent the height on drawing it until you want it.

7. WHAT I HAVE NOT TOUCHED: the assistant panel and everything in it, what a meeting actually does, the tools it consults, the journal schema, the migration, or any of the wording the model itself produces. This is the screen only.

8. THE ROW FOR A MOVE ALREADY DONE keeps its place in the list rather than dropping to the bottom. A plan is a sequence and some moves say "after the chase"; re-ordering it as you work would break that. It greys instead. If you would rather done work got out of the way, that is a different rule and I would want to hear it before writing it.

THE TWO STATES THAT MUST NOT LOOK BROKEN →

A — NO MEETING HELD YET. The old screen paints "Hold the meeting" in accent red, then rewrites the text and demotes the button to grey a moment later when the journal answers — the main action of the screen changing under your eyes on every visit. Here the un-held state is a real empty state in the plan panel: it names what a meeting is, what it costs, and that it never runs itself, and the accent is on the one act. The strip stays, because it is counted from the books and not from the meeting — only "meetings held" goes grey and says "none today". The scoreboard, the questions and the playbook all stay, because none of them came from this morning.

The footer says the last meeting was yesterday and how much of it got done. That is the fact the old screen buried three sections down.

B — THE JOURNAL CANNOT BE READ. The migration is not applied, so nothing is kept. A failure must name itself: crimson, what is lost (advice, the account, the scoreboard, the record), and the exact remedy — the file to paste and where. Then the plan the current session DID produce, marked "held this session — not kept", because a plan you can still act on today is worth showing even though it will not survive the page closing.

What is deliberately NOT drawn in state B: the strip, the switch and the record. There is nothing behind them, and an empty scoreboard reads as a manager that has promised nothing rather than one that cannot remember. Named rather than dropped.

THE PHONE — its own design, not the desk reflowed

820px is a switch, so this is drawn from scratch at 390: 44px navy bar, 26px Archivo Black page name, 15px body, 44px hit targets, 60px white tab bar. No fake status bar and no fake keyboard — the real ones render on top of your layout.

THE FIELD IS FIRST. On the console "Talk to it" is a button in the page header; here it is a field, because a button says a thing and a field asks for one, and this screen's whole argument is that the brain is something you talk to. It is not the accent — a field is not an act.

THE STRIP IS 2×2 and drops "meetings held", which is the least useful of the five in a yard.

THE MOVE IS A CARD, not a row: 15px name, the reasoning at reading size, the money at 19px mono, and two 44px actions. The accent is the first card's action — the one thing to do next, exactly as on the desk. Everything below it is ghost.

A DONE MOVE CARRIES NO BUTTONS. It carries the verdigris line saying when. Nothing on this screen ever looks like it acted by itself.

THE TAB BAR'S FIVE MARKS are drawn for this shop — a sunrise, a price tag, a note with a coin, a bubble speaking, a stack of sheets — and the active one is FILLED where the others are stroked, because a shape change reads at arm's length and a colour change alone does not.
